meta.regime: The Middle East shock has split into two separate transmission channels and only one of them is priced. The oil channel is mature - Brent at 99.477 and WTI at 94.342 are six-week highs, the central banks have all written it into their statements, and the FX board has already repriced around it. The GAS channel is younger, faster and pointed almost entirely at Europe: QatarEnergy's force majeure now runs into November, EU storage is at a record seasonal low, and European gas is up 28% in a month against crude's 15%. That makes the euro and sterling the currencies absorbing a terms-of-trade tax their central banks cannot offset, and it arrives one day before the ECB publishes new projections. Underneath it, China quietly reflated overnight, which repairs the commodity leg the Antipodeans lost last week.

dailyRead: The single most important thing that changed overnight is not in any central bank's remit and is not being traded as an FX story yet. European gas is 78.12 euros per MWh, up 3.01% on the session, 6.03% on the week and 28.42% on the MONTH; UK gas is 194.46 pence per therm, up 3.00% today and 29.82% on the month; German gas is 77.00 euros and up 23.96% on the month. For comparison, crude - the shock everyone is watching - is up 14.84% on the month. Gas is running at roughly double the pace of oil and almost nobody is pricing it into the currencies. The mechanism is now explicit rather than speculative: QatarEnergy has extended its LNG force majeure, originally running through September, into early NOVEMBER, after Iran continued to attack Qatari-linked carriers; Italy's Edison alone has lost 29 cargoes since April, about 3.8 billion cubic metres. EU contracted volumes with Qatar for 2026 are around 21.5 bcm, roughly 6.3% of annual EU-27 demand, and Europe is trying to replace that with almost no Russian pipeline gas while storage sits at 65-66% full - the lowest seasonal level in records going back to 2009 against a long-run average near 83%. Utilities delayed buying on the assumption Qatar would resume; that bet has now failed twice. The FX consequence is a terms-of-trade tax falling almost entirely on the euro and sterling, and it lands 24 hours before the ECB. Euro-area August energy inflation had ALREADY jumped to 14.3% from 10.3%, which is what took HICP to 3.3%, the highest since September 2023 - and that print was taken before this week's further 6% weekly rise in TTF. So tomorrow's meeting has a structure yesterday's file did not fully describe. The 25 basis points to a 2.50% deposit facility is not the event; markets price it at 99% and TE carries consensus and forecast at 2.65% on the refi. Two things are the event. First, the NEW STAFF PROJECTIONS, where the staff inflation path can be revised UP into a market that has already decided the cycle is finished - the September 3 Reuters poll had 91% seeing 2.50% as the year-end rate and 78% seeing it held through mid-2027. Second, guidance, and here this file must adjust: the preview consensus that has formed since yesterday is that Lagarde retains FULL OPTIONALITY and offers no firm path, which is a materially softer outcome than treating the terminal as closed. Yesterday's file called the forward path shut on the strength of that poll; the honest correction is that economists have closed it, the ECB has not, and Lagarde speaks TODAY at 17:00Z before she says anything tomorrow. EUR therefore holds +1 with a genuinely two-sided distribution - a hawkish projection round is the upside, and the gas tax on euro-area activity is the downside, and they roughly cancel. The second change is China, and it is a repair rather than a deterioration. Chinese CPI rose 0.8% year-on-year in August from 0.5%, matching consensus, with the monthly rate at +0.4% from -0.1%; PPI rose 3.8% from 3.5%, BEATING the 3.7% consensus and accelerating; and yesterday's trade data showed exports +25% year-on-year against 23.9% prior. This file spent yesterday's session using the import miss - 28.2% against a 30% consensus - as one of four legs behind the kiwi downgrade. That leg is now weaker: producer prices accelerating out of deflation with exports beating is a demand signal, and it is the first clean one in weeks. The practical effect is that the commodity leg under both Antipodeans is repaired, which is why the kiwi's three-session slide STOPPED today - NZD/USD is 0.58579, up 0.07%, and up 0.16% on the week rather than extending. NZD nonetheless HOLDS at MINUS 1, because the leg that actually justified the downgrade was never the China number. It was the RBNZ, and that leg got firmer overnight rather than softer: ANZ's read of the September statement is that the policy track does NOT point to another increase in October and that the language around future decisions was deliberately vague and highly conditional, which is why wholesale rates and the kiwi fell after a HIKE. A central bank that raises to 2.75% and then refuses to validate the next move is the definition of a currency that does not get paid for its carry. TE still shows October 28 unchanged with the next 25bp only on December 9. The third item is a correction this file owes on the dollar, and it should be stated plainly rather than buried. Yesterday's file reported that Fed pricing had 'drifted to roughly a coin flip near 50-60%' and cited a tracker at 49.4% hike against 50.6% hold. That number was from prediction markets - Kalshi at 48% and Polymarket at 49% - not from rate markets. CME FedWatch was 58.7% on September 7 and is near 56% now. So the drift from the 66% carried on August 31 is real but SMALLER than yesterday reported, and the correct current read for September 16 is a modest hike lean, not a coin flip. Nothing in the data moved: payrolls +162,000 with 55,000 of upward revisions, unemployment 4.1%, CPI 3.4% with the monthly rate at 0.1%, GDP 2.1% annual, non-manufacturing PMI 55.4, services 56.5, against consumer confidence at 51.7 and retail sales -0.6%. USD holds +1. What this changes tactically is the composition of the USD/JPY short: it rests on the JAPANESE leg, not on a decayed Fed, and that leg is the strongest on the board. Japan added three more confirmations overnight. Final Q2 GDP was revised UP - 0.4% quarter-on-quarter against a 0.3% flash, annualised 1.4% against a 1.1% consensus, with capital expenditure revised to -0.9% from -1.2% - so corporate spending is more resilient than the flash implied. The Reuters Tankan index rose to 21 from 18 against a forecast of 15. Machine tool orders rose 64.7% year-on-year from 50.4%, against a 43% forecast. That sits on top of Monday's wage print - average cash earnings +4.7% year-on-year, the fastest since 1997, with real wages +2.4% for a seventh consecutive month - and a current account that swung to PLUS 2,989 billion yen. Market pricing for September 18 is now reported near 80%, and more importantly overnight index swaps imply roughly 75 basis points of CUMULATIVE tightening by April 2027, which is the market beginning to price the thing this file has flagged as underowned: Takata's argument that the Bank should move nimbly, with outsized moves above 25bp and back-to-back hikes both explicitly named as possibilities, reportedly reinforced by comments from US Treasury Secretary Bessent. USD/JPY is 153.225, down 0.49% today, 3.53% on the week and 3.88% on the month, the lowest since February. JPY holds +3 and it is the only score on this board that is not a compromise. Australia holds +2 and today the argument is cleaner than yesterday's. The copper story stops being purely a supply story: with Chinese PPI accelerating to 3.8% and exports at +25%, the metal at 6.6997 USD per pound - down 0.58% today but up 3.06% on the week - now has a demand leg under it as well as the Codelco, Freeport and Congo supply disruptions. AUD/USD is 0.72314, up 0.20% today, 0.88% on the week, 2.51% on the month and 8.38% year-to-date, which is the best major on every horizon beyond a day. Against that the domestic softening is real and got worse: Westpac consumer confidence fell 5.2% to 84.4 and NAB business confidence slipped to MINUS 8 from MINUS 6. The cash rate is 4.35%, the G10 high, September 29 sits near 54%, trimmed mean is stuck at 3.6% and the monthly inflation rate jumped +1.0%. Canada holds +1 with the oil leg at its strongest of the cycle - Brent at 99.477, up 1.59% today and 4.00% on the week, genuinely knocking on 100 dollars, and WTI at 94.342, up 1.41% and 14.84% on the month. The current account is PLUS C$8,800 million, business confidence 64.3 from 55.1, and Q2 growth annualised at 3.3%. The reason this is not an upgrade is unchanged and specific: August employment fell 41,700 and average hourly wages decelerated to 2.0% year-on-year from 2.8%, and it is the wage number rather than the headline that governs the BoC's reaction function. USD/CAD is 1.37732, down 0.07%. Switzerland holds +1 on the same terms as yesterday - a manufacturing PMI at 57.1 from 53.2, a current account at CHF 15,544 million, August CPI at 0.8% and Q2 annual growth at 2.3% - with the SNB's stated readiness to intervene the reason it is not a +2, and Iran's tanker retaliation making that language more likely to be repeated on September 24, not less. USD/CHF 0.80834, -0.13%. Sterling holds MINUS 1, and the position deserves an honest performance note: cable is 1.35574, UP 0.12% today and 0.54% on the WEEK, so the short is not paying against the dollar and GBP/USD is downgraded to LOW-MED accordingly. The structural case is intact - the highest borrowing costs of any G10 developed nation, July borrowing 69% above the prior year, debt at 94.3% of GDP, a Bank about 90% priced to hold at 3.75% on September 17 after the DMP survey cut one-year firm CPI expectations to 3.1% - and the UK data improved only at the margin, with consumer confidence to MINUS 14 from MINUS 17 and annual GDP to 1.2% from 0.9% against a quarterly rate that slowed to 0.4%. What sterling now has that it did not have yesterday is the worst gas exposure in G10, up 29.82% on the month into a confirmed October Ofgem cap rise, which is stagflationary rather than hawkish for a Bank that has already frozen. Express sterling against the yen and the euro, not against the dollar.

geopolitics: The war now has two transmission channels into FX and only one of them is priced. The OIL channel is mature. The tanker war became fully two-sided over the past week: US Central Command permanently disabled the IRGC crude carriers M/T Downy off the coast of Kharg Island and M/T Stark 1 near Jask, and completely destroyed the unladen crude tanker M/T Kylo in the Gulf of Oman, striking it repeatedly to render it inoperable - retaliation for IRGC ballistic missiles fired at a US aircraft carrier and a destroyer, neither of which was hit and with no injuries. Analysts read Iran's willingness to target two US carriers as a calculated escalation rather than a miscalculation, and the fighting is increasingly playing out at sea with both sides contesting control of the Strait itself. Iran's Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei's formally declared restricted zone - running from the US naval blockade line, through the Strait, and into the Persian Gulf, with ships entering without Tehran's coordination added to Iran's sanctions list, affecting insurance cover and future passage - is now the standing legal instrument alongside the military one. Brent is 99.477, up 1.59% on the session and 4.00% on the week, genuinely knocking on 100 dollars; WTI is 94.342, up 1.41% today, 3.64% on the week and 14.84% on the month. The countervailing facts are unchanged: transits still run above nine million barrels a day against roughly twenty million before the conflict, so much of the disruption is in the price, the US has cleared the strait of mines and degraded Iran's ability to re-lay them, workarounds keep expanding, and OPEC has cut its 2026 demand growth estimate to 580,000 bpd from 780,000. USOIL stays LONG at HIGH. The GAS channel is the one this file thinks is being underpriced, and it is now running at roughly DOUBLE the pace of oil. EU gas is 78.12 euros per MWh, up 3.01% on the session, 6.03% on the week and 28.42% on the MONTH; UK gas is 194.4617 pence per therm and up 29.82% on the month; German gas is 77.00 euros and up 23.96%. Crude, by comparison, is up 14.84%. The driver is no longer speculative: QatarEnergy has extended its LNG force majeure - originally running through September - into early NOVEMBER, after Iran continued to attack Qatar and Qatari-linked LNG carriers. Italy's Edison alone has lost 29 cargoes since force majeure was activated in April, roughly 3.8 billion cubic metres. EU contracted volumes with Qatar for 2026 are around 21.5 bcm, about 6.3% of EU-27 annual demand, and Europe must replace that with almost no Russian pipeline gas while storage sits at 65-66% full - the lowest seasonal level in records going back to 2009, against a long-run average near 83%. Utilities and traders delayed purchases twice on the assumption Qatar would resume; that bet has now failed twice. Six FX consequences follow. First, and most important today: the gas shock is a terms-of-trade TAX falling almost entirely on the euro and sterling, and unlike the oil shock it is not something a rate hike offsets - it raises the CPI path while cutting real household income. That is why EUR stays at +1 despite a 99%-priced hike tomorrow, and why the sterling case survives even though cable is up 0.54% on the week. Second, it lands 24 hours before the ECB, and it cuts hawkish on the projections and dovish on growth at the same time: euro-area August energy inflation had already jumped to 14.3% from 10.3%, taking HICP to 3.3%, the highest since September 2023 - and that print predates this week's further 6% rise in TTF, so the new staff inflation path can be revised UP into a market that has decided the cycle is finished. Third, GER40 is downgraded from RANGE to SHORT: an industrial economy entering winter with a 24% monthly rise in its gas input cost, a central bank hiking into it, and Brent near 100 dollars is a worse combination than the Q2 growth revision offsets. Fourth, the franc gains a second bid that the SNB will not welcome - with 0% rates and no euro-area-scale gas import bill, CHF is the cleanest European hedge against exactly this shock, which is part of why EUR/CHF keeps failing to rally and why the SNB's June intervention language is more likely to be repeated on September 24. Fifth, the yen's terms-of-trade objection is now the weakest it has been: Japan still imports essentially all its energy and the trade balance at MINUS 634 billion yen is the last surviving leg of this file's old bearish caveat, but the current account has swung to PLUS 2,989 billion, retail sales printed +2.4% m/m, real wages have risen for seven straight months, and final Q2 GDP was revised up - Japanese households are absorbing the energy shock rather than being crushed by it, which is why the BoJ can hike into it. Sixth, the whole tightening board still rests on this one input and the central banks say so explicitly - the RBA's August minutes list Middle East oil FIRST among the hike arguments, the BoC's September statement flags the continuation of the war as an upside inflation risk, the RBNZ attributes its 4.1% inflation largely to Middle East fuel prices, and the ECB accounts cite Middle East upside risk. Four reaction functions from one input, which is also why the entire board would reprice together on a credible de-escalation headline. That single headline remains the largest correlated risk across every position in this file.
